12222-the-faithful-shepherdess-the-works:
John Fletcher pastoral play The Faithful Shepherdess appears here in the Cambridge edition of Beaumont and Fletcher works, volume two of ten. First performed around 1608, the play failed on stage in its day, yet later readers prized its verse.

Clorin, a shepherdess who has buried her love in an arbor, vows chastity and practices herbal healing by his grave. Around her, shepherds and shepherdesses chase, refuse, and mistake each other, while Pan and satyrs hover at the edges. Fletcher mixes lyric beauty with frank talk of desire, and the play tests whether constancy can survive in a world of appetite. The edition gives a clean text for a play that rewards reading more than performance.
12933-little-journeys-to-the-homes-of-th:
Elbert Hubbard's Little Journeys to the Homes of the Great, memorial edition of 1916, gathers monthly pilgrimages begun in 1894 and kept up for fourteen years without a break. One hundred eighty journeys visit the homes of men and women who changed thought, empire, and civilization, in Hubbard's warm, chatty style. The Roycrofters printed the book at East Aurora.

A Turner passage shows the method: a boy artist, helped by Doctor Munro into the Royal Academy at fourteen, sells few pictures while rivals scorn his ragged genius. Hubbard turns each life into a short, moral tale. The volume remains a charming introduction to great lives for general readers.
13619-little-journeys-to-the-homes-of-th:
Elbert Hubbard's Little Journeys to the Homes of English Authors, volume five of 1916, visits William Morris. Robert Browning, Alfred Tennyson, Robert Burns, John Milton, Samuel Johnson, Macaulay, Byron, Addison, Southey, Coleridge, and Disraeli. Each journey blends life, home, and work into a short, vivid portrait.

Morris sings as the idle singer who cannot ease fear or make death little. A woman cured by the Healer loves him wildly after feeding and warming a cold, hungry, homeless man. Byron at Cambridge from 1805 to 1808 perfects shooting, swimming, fencing, drinking, and gambling, then lives at sleepy, gossipy Southwell under wholesome restraint. Hubbard writes literary pilgrimage with warmth and anecdote.
13778-little-journeys-to-the-homes-of-th:
Elbert Hubbard's Little Journeys, in this Roycroft memorial edition, profiles famous women. Elizabeth Barrett Browning, Madame Guyon, Harriet Martineau, and Charlotte Brontë lead the list. Christina Rossetti, Rosa Bonheur, Madame de Staël, and Elizabeth Fry follow. Mary Lamb, Jane Austen, Empress Josephine, and Mary Shelley close it.

Hubbard writes short, warm lives that stress character and work. He opens with his creed: put heart into the work done for bread. Each sketch mixes biography with moral reflection and anecdote. The Roycrofters printed the volume at East Aurora, New York, in 1916. The book suits readers who enjoy brief, inspiring lives of notable women.
13911-little-journeys-to-the-homes-of-th:
Elbert Hubbard's third Little Journeys volume profiles American statesmen. George Washington, Benjamin Franklin, Thomas Jefferson, and Samuel Adams lead. John Hancock, John Quincy Adams, Alexander Hamilton, and Daniel Webster follow. Henry Clay, John Jay, William H. Seward, and Abraham Lincoln close the list.

Hubbard debunks Weems' cherry-tree tales, calling them untruthful Sunday-school romance. He praises patience, work, and character over legend. Each sketch blends life story with moral comment in Hubbard's brisk style. The Roycroft memorial edition appeared in 1916. The volume suits readers who want short, lively lives of founders.
15480-new-york-times-current-history-the:
This June 1915 number of Current History, the New York Times monthly magazine, is dominated by the Lusitania case. It prints President Wilson's speeches and note to Germany, with a history of attacks on American lives in the German war zone. Maps, official reports, and a first cabin list support the record.

Survivors describe the submarine crew observed, the death of Charles Frohman, and the heroic end of Alfred Vanderbilt, while Klein and Hubbard are lost. German reports justify the deed, a British coroner's verdict answers, and Captain Turner testifies. The number captures a turning point in American feeling: a civilian sinking, told in documents, that moved the United States closer to war.
18118-little-journeys-to-the-homes-of-th:
Elbert Hubbard wrote Little Journeys to the Homes of Eminent Painters, volume four of his Little Journeys, printed in 1916 by the Roycrofters at East Aurora. Hubbard, the Roycroft founder, made these small books by hand, and they sold widely as popular lives.

The volume sketches Michelangelo, Rembrandt, Rubens, Meissonier, Titian, Van Dyck, Fortuny, Scheffer, Millet, Reynolds, Landseer, and Doré. Hubbard opens with Michelangelo's sonnet on marble that outlives its maker. His prose is warm, chatty, and moral. It is a pleasant, old-style gallery of painters, best for readers who like lives told as tales.
18616-moral-principles-and-medical-pract:
Rev. Charles Coppens, a Jesuit professor at Creighton Medical College in Omaha, published this volume at New York in 1897 with Benziger Brothers. It treats the moral rules that should guide doctors, as the base of medical jurisprudence. Coppens argues that leading doctors already hold sound principles, but students need them taught more plainly and firmly.

The book, approved by Jesuit censors and the Archbishop of New York, is dedicated to John A. Creighton, founder of the college and St. Joseph's Hospital. It aims to shape young physicians in conscience as well as skill. The volume is a clear window on Catholic medical ethics of its day.
18866-scientific-american-volume-40-no-1:
This number of the Scientific American, volume forty, number thirteen, dated New York, March 29, 1879, calls itself a weekly journal of practical information, art, science, mechanics, chemistry, and manufactures. Munn and Company edited and published it from Park Row, at three dollars and twenty cents a year, postage paid.

Its contents range from Africa crossed again and Peter Cooper as an inventor to aluminum, banana flour, snow-raised bread, and the domestication of the buffalo. Illustrated pieces cover a novel ore crusher, an improved door bolt, and a furnace for burning garbage, with notes on pneumatic clocks, chimney flues, and carpet beetles. The issue shows a young industrial America trading workshop news week by week.
18936-little-journeys-to-the-homes-of-th:
A 1916 memorial edition of Elbert Hubbard's Little Journeys to the Homes of Great Teachers gathers short biographical essays on twelve figures held up as teachers of humankind. The volume opens with Moses and moves through Confucius, Pythagoras, Plato, King Alfred, Erasmus, Booker T. Washington, Thomas Arnold, Friedrich Froebel, Hypatia, Saint Benedict, and Mary Baker Eddy.

Each essay blends life story with moral reflection, presenting its subject as a model of character and influence rather than as a scholarly biography. Hubbard praises Moses, for instance, for practical wisdom in hygiene, order, industry, and government, as well as for insight into human nature. The book offers an early twentieth-century popular canon of teaching lives, spanning ancient lawgivers and philosophers, medieval rulers and monks, and modern educators and reformers.
19080-little-journeys-to-the-homes-of-th:
Elbert Hubbard wrote this 1916 volume of Little Journeys to the homes of great scientists, printed by the Roycrofters at East Aurora. It profiles Newton, Galileo, Copernicus, Humboldt, Herschel, Darwin, Haeckel, Linnaeus, Huxley, Tyndall, Wallace, and Fiske. Each life is told with warmth and anecdote.

Young Newton, meant to be a farmer, buys Descartes' Geometry with his market money, builds water clocks, sundials, and kites with lanterns, and lets cows stray into corn while he dreams. Such tales humanise genius. Readers get lively, readable lives of science, meant to inspire rather than to weigh evidence.
20318-little-journeys-to-the-homes-of-th:
Little Journeys to the Homes of the Great, volume fourteen, visits poets in their homes. Elbert Hubbard's series took readers to the houses of famed figures. One passage scorns cheap jokes about mothers-in-law and step-parents alike. It praises Wagner's stepfather as a patient, loving, loyal friend.

Another note honors a writer who called his mother-in-law his best friend. She always came when needed and stayed while work remained. Home life, in this volume, shapes the poets as much as verse. Readers get warm, chatty visits with great writers in their daily rooms.
23458-little-journeys-to-the-homes-of-th:
Elbert Hubbard devoted this thirteenth volume of his Little Journeys to great lovers, in a nineteen sixteen memorial edition. Robert Louis Stevenson and Fanny Osbourne lead, followed by Josiah and Sarah Wedgwood, William Godwin and Mary Wollstonecraft, Dante and Beatrice, and John Stuart Mill and Harriet Taylor.

Parnell and Kitty O'Shea, Petrarch and Laura, Rossetti and Elizabeth Siddal, Balzac and Madame Hanska, Fenelon and Madame Guyon, Lassalle and Helene von Donniges, and Nelson and Lady Hamilton complete the set. Hubbard opens with a Stevenson household prayer for love, peace, work, and friends, then sketches each pair with warmth and moral comment. Readers get brief, readable lives of love in many ages, told as visits to homes rather than as dry history.
23595-little-journeys-to-the-homes-of-th:
Elbert Hubbard devoted this eleventh volume of his Little Journeys to great businessmen, in a nineteen sixteen memorial edition. Robert Owen leads, with his claim that he spent his surplus wealth to the last shilling on industrial betterment, never a pound on profligacy or luxury, despite a prelate's charge.

James Oliver, Stephen Girard, Mayer A. Rothschild, Philip D. Armour, John J. Astor, Peter Cooper, Andrew Carnegie, George Peabody, A. T. Stewart, H. H. Rogers, and James J. Hill follow, each sketched as a visit to a home and a life. Hubbard writes with warmth and moral comment, praising thrift, daring, and giving in turn. Readers who like brief business lives will enjoy the set as a gallery of builders, bankers, and givers who shaped American wealth.
24308-poetry-for-poetry-s-sake-an-inaugu:
A. C. Bradley, professor of poetry at the University of Oxford and formerly fellow of Balliol College, gave this inaugural lecture on June 5, 1901, printed at the Clarendon Press almost as delivered. Bradley notes that difficult subjects are treated too summarily in the early pages, since full exposition would destroy the lecture's form. He comes to speak of poetry, not of himself.

Restored after twenty years to the university that taught him and where he first tried teaching, Bradley recalls a predecessor. That predecessor wrote exquisite verse on Oxford's beauty, and prose on her illusions, set against her long war with the Philistine. He will not praise his predecessors for five years of lecturing ahead. Readers get a classic defense of poetry valued for its own sake.
26377-new-york-times-current-history-the:
This July 1915 issue of the New York Times magazine Current History records the European War as Americans read about it month by month. The Lusitania case leads the number, with President Wilson's reply to Berlin, Germany's press opinion, and comment from the Allies. It also covers William J. Bryan's resignation as Secretary of State, his defense, and the debate over a league to enforce peace.

Battle reports follow from Galicia, where Przemysl and Lemberg changed hands, from Belgium, France, and the Dardanelles campaign, along with pieces on Italy's entry against Austria-Hungary and Britain's munitions drive. Cartoons, a war chronology, and essays such as The Belgian War Mothers close the issue. It stands as a primary source for the war's first year.
6306-little-journeys-to-the-homes-of-the:
Elbert Hubbard's sixth volume of Little Journeys visits the homes of eminent artists, from Raphael and Leonardo to Botticelli, Thorwaldsen, and Gainsborough. Velasquez, Corot, Correggio, Bellini, Cellini, Abbey, and Whistler complete the dozen. Raphael, Hubbard notes, knew only one self imposed limit, beauty, and though his life was short, his work stays imperishable and free from mannerism.

Each journey mixes life, work, and moral, as Hubbard walks the reader through studios and streets where great pictures were made. Thorwaldsen's studio draws daily visitors to a reception room of casts, and his good fortune, a smile that disarmed furies, follows him through grief. The volume is Hubbard's popular art history, warm, anecdotal, and built to send readers back to the pictures themselves.
6449-little-journeys-to-the-homes-of-the:
Elbert Hubbard's ninth Little Journeys volume visits the homes of great reformers. Its twelve lives are John Wesley, Henry George, Garibaldi, Richard Cobden, Thomas Paine, John Knox, John Bright, Bradlaugh, Theodore Parker, Oliver Cromwell, Anne Hutchinson, and Jean Jacques Rousseau. Wesley opens, lame horse and aching head, suddenly thinking God can heal man or beast as he will, and finding weariness and headache ceased.

Hubbard notes Burke's remark that Susanna Wesley was her parents' twenty fourth child, then wonders what church history would have lost had their twenty third child been named Omega. A later passage praises Britain for strength in resources, courage, institutions, and position, arguing she can afford to be moral before other European powers. Hubbard writes reformers as neighbours, vivid, anecdotal, and fond of a pointed moral.
8952-scientific-american-volume-22-no-1-:
Scientific American, volume twenty-two, number one, January 1, 1870, presents itself as a weekly journal of practical information, art, science, mechanics, chemistry. Manufactures, at three dollars per annum in advance. Contents include engines of the Spanish gunboats, the torpedo problem, sugar making in Louisiana, sticking or court plaster, an improved hoisting pulley wanted. Ferdinand de Lesseps, chief promoter of the Suez Canal. An ingenious vent peg, a new English patent pulley block, plants in sleeping rooms, improved treadle motion, and an improved method of catching curculios follow.

Illustrated articles, marked with asterisks, show the journal's visual, workshop character. The 1870 number captures American ingenuity on the eve of the Gilded Age: canals, gunboats, sugar, and small inventions side by side. Historians of technology will find a rich weekly record, and general readers a reminder of how ordinary Americans once learned science, one practical article at a time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-marqu:
Jesuit missionary Jacques Marquette explored the Mississippi River country. He was born at Laon in north-central France in 1636. He died near Ludington, Michigan, on 19 May 1675. He came from an ancient family noted for civic and military service. At seventeen he entered the Society of Jesus. After twelve years of study and teaching in French Jesuit colleges, he was sent in 1666 to Canada's Indian missions.

Arriving at Quebec, he was assigned to Three Rivers on the St Lawrence. There he assisted Druillettes and studied the Huron language as preparation. His gift for languages let him converse fluently in six dialects. Recalled to Quebec in spring 1668, he went to Montreal. There he awaited the flotilla bound for his first western mission. After eighteen months of western labor, he set out on the river journey that made his name. The entry opens a missionary-explorer's career.
doe-osti-3453385-convergence-analysis-of: Metals bend differently depending on how fast you push them — that's rate-dependent plasticity. Elmer and Lester analyze whether the math for J2 plasticity, a standard metal-deformation model, actually converges to the right answer. The analysis tells simulators when to trust their numbers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AutopsyJFKProto: Autopsy Protocol - Clinical Record (CD-362A): the OCR of the clinical autopsy protocol form dated November 22, 1963 - heavily garbled, with the form's structure barely visible. A damaged capture, preserved as found, complete. From the archive's collection.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BarkhamJohnFram: In April 1971 the New York Times received this letter to the editor over the King assassination. The letter disputes a review by John Barkham touching on the claim that James Earl Ray was framed, a question then fresh in print. The author's name cannot be recovered from the garbled text. The letter survives as a bit of the public argument over Ray's guilt that ran in the newspapers for years after Memphis.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BrianVJ_Brian_V: Dallas Police Special Service Bureau Memorandum: the garbled OCR of a Dallas Police Department memorandum - a photocopy, date unclear. A damaged capture, kept as found. A fragment. Unreadable in parts. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HobbsEugeneJ_Ho: An FBI memorandum dated May 21, 1964 went from the Office of the Director to J. Lee Rankin, general counsel of the Warren Commission. Its subject was the Central Intelligence Agency. Traffic between the Bureau's top office and the commission's lawyer ran constantly that spring, and this memo's subject put the CIA on that channel.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JolingRobertJ_J:
Attorney Robert J. Joling wrote an article with a verdict in its title: The Murder of Robert Kennedy Is Still Unsolved. Joling reconstructs the assassination of Senator Kennedy in the pantry of the Ambassador Hotel. From that reconstruction he argues the case was never truly closed, and he calls for further investigation.

A lawyer's reconstruction works like a brief, marshaling shots, witnesses, and timing toward a conclusion. Joling believed the official account left the pantry unexplained. His article preserves the legal case for reopening, addressed to readers rather than to a court.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JusticeDepartme: A letter dated August 20, 1970 was addressed to Attorney General John N. Mitchell, who ran the Justice Department under President Nixon. The letter is filed with the department's correspondence in this archive. The surviving record gives the date and the addressee but not the writer or the subject, so the entry stands as a dated letter to the nation's chief law officer.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PlaineJamesJ_Pl: From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers. An obscure item, complete. A bare file, kept as issued. Subject: government records. nsia-PlaineJamesJ Plaine James J: the made public government document, captured as titled.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RoehrightJoachi: nsia-RoehrightJoachimRudolph Roehright Joachim Rudolph: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RomeroJoseLuisC:
The French magazine KIO published an exclusive on October 2, 1972, under the headline 'Cet homme devait tuer Kennedy à Paris': this man was to kill Kennedy in Paris. The piece, by Philippe Bernert, presents a confession made to Camille Gilles. The man confessing was a former officer of the 5th REP, a French parachute regiment. He said he had been assigned to assassinate Kennedy in Paris.

Confessions of almost-assassins were a European magazine staple of the era. Bernert's exclusive gives one in full dress: a regiment, a handler, a plot that never fired. The article preserves the claim as the magazine sold it. Readers can weigh the telling against the record, which contains no such Paris attempt, while seeing exactly how the story was framed.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SeigenthalerJoh:
John J. Hollins reviewed 'A Search for Justice,' a book by John Seigenthaler, James Squires, John Hemphill, and Frank Ritter. The four authors built their book on three famous trials of 1969: Clay Shaw in New Orleans, James Earl Ray in Memphis, and Sirhan Bishara Sirhan in Los Angeles. Hollins calls it a hard-hitting attack on American justice.

Three assassinations produced three prosecutions, and 1969 judged all of them. A book by four journalists arguing that the system failed in each case had a ready audience. The review weighs that argument and the reporting under it. It preserves the book's reception: praised as an attack, by name, on the justice that tried the decade's most watched defendants.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SmithMJ_Smith_M:
M. J. Smith wrote to Harold Weisberg on March 6, 1974, with a reader's question. Smith asks where he can obtain Weisberg's books. He names three: 'Whitewash II,' 'Photographic Whitewash,' and 'Oswald in New Orleans.' All were self-published works, sold by mail from the author's house rather than through bookstores.

A letter like Smith's shows the distribution problem of dissenting publishing. The books existed, reviewers had quarreled over them, and a reader in 1974 still had to write to the author to find a copy. Weisberg's mail was full of such requests, and answering them was part of his work. The letter preserves the titles a reader wanted, eleven years after Dallas, in the order he asked for them.
little-journeys-to-the-homes-of-the-grea:
Elbert Hubbard began his Little Journeys series in 1894. One pilgrimage appeared monthly for fourteen years without a break. The Roycrofters printed this Memorial Edition in East Aurora in 1916. Volume One visits the homes of good men and great.

One hundred eighty journeys appeared across the whole series. Publisher's praise compares Hubbard's set to Plutarch's parallel lives. His subjects transformed thought and changed empires, the preface claims. Hubbard himself had died before this memorial printing appeared. Wm. H. Wise joined the Roycrofters as New York publishers. Fourteen years of monthly pilgrimages built the famous series.

Hubbard's second Little Journeys volume visits famous women. Elizabeth Barrett Browning leads the contents list. Madame Guyon, Harriet Martineau, and Charlotte Brontë follow. Christina Rossetti and Rosa Bonheur represent poetry and painting.

Madame de Staël, Elizabeth Fry, and Mary Lamb appear later. Jane Austen, Empress Josephine, and Mary Shelley close the roster. Bert Hubbard contributes a sketch of his father, Elbert Hubbard. A Ruskin epigraph urges doing delightful work heartily, not by halves. A Bert Hubbard sketch of his father opens the volume. Work worth doing deserves heart and will, Ruskin insists.

Volume Three of Hubbard's journeys visits American statesmen at home. George Washington leads a roster of founding figures. Benjamin Franklin, Thomas Jefferson, and Samuel Adams follow. John Hancock and John Quincy Adams represent Massachusetts strongly.

Alexander Hamilton and John Jay bring the Federalist era in. Daniel Webster, Henry Clay, and William Seward continue the line. Abraham Lincoln closes the volume's patriotic gallery. A camp scene and Bert Hubbard's sketch open the book. The Little Journeys camp fronts the statesmen's portraits here. Patience, charity, and devotion open Hubbard's camp motto. Seward and Lincoln bring the statesmen's story into the Civil War years.

Hubbard devotes Volume Four to eminent painters' homes. Michelangelo leads the contents, followed by Rembrandt and Rubens. Meissonier, Titian, and Anthony Van Dyck continue the old masters. Fortuny, Ary Scheffer, and François Millet bring modern schools in.

Joshua Reynolds, Landseer, and Gustave Doré close the list. A Michelangelo sonnet on art outliving nature opens his chapter. Hubbard mixes biography, home description, and warm admiration. Each painter receives one self-contained little journey for readers. Centuries hence, the sonnet promises, beauty and sadness will show together. Landseer's animals and Doré's engravings broaden the painters' range.

English authors fill Hubbard's fifth volume of little journeys. William Morris leads, then Robert Browning and Alfred Tennyson. Robert Burns and John Milton bring older centuries in. Samuel Johnson and Thomas Macaulay represent prose authority.

Lord Byron, Joseph Addison, and Robert Southey follow in order. Samuel Taylor Coleridge and Benjamin Disraeli close the contents. Morris's Idle Singer poem sounds a weary opening note. Hubbard tours homes to make great writers feel near and human. The idle singer cannot ease the burden of readers' fears. Hubbard prints Morris's poem before touring the poet's home.

Volume Six of Hubbard's journeys turns to eminent artists. Raphael leads a contents list rich in Renaissance names. Leonardo, Botticelli, and Thorwaldsen follow the first chapter. Gainsborough, Velázquez, and Corot widen the European range.

Correggio, Bellini, and Cellini represent Italian art's golden age. Abbey and Whistler bring the list toward Hubbard's own time. A Wilhelm Lübke quotation praises Raphael's purity and freedom. Hubbard's sketches aim to bring each artist's home life close. Hubbard's own era enters through Abbey and Whistler at the end. Lubke praises Raphael's freedom from superficiality and mannerism.

Great reformers fill the ninth volume of Hubbard's journeys. John Wesley leads the contents, followed by Henry George. Garibaldi, Richard Cobden, and Thomas Paine bring politics in. John Knox and John Bright represent pulpit and Parliament.

Bradlaugh, Theodore Parker, and Oliver Cromwell continue the roster. Anne Hutchinson and Jean Jacques Rousseau close the list. Wesley's journal opens his chapter with a lame horse healed. Hubbard admires reformers who changed thought by force of character. Susanna Wesley was the twenty-fourth child of her parents, Burke noted. John himself was fifteenth among nineteen Wesley children.

Hubbard's tenth volume journeys to the homes of great teachers. Moses leads a list spanning scripture, philosophy, and schools. Confucius, Pythagoras, and Plato represent ancient wisdom. King Alfred and Erasmus carry teaching into medieval Europe.

Booker T. Washington appears among the modern educators. Thomas Arnold and Friedrich Froebel represent school and kindergarten. Hypatia, Saint Benedict, and Mary Baker Eddy close the contents. The Roycrofters issued this Memorial Edition in 1916. East Aurora's Roycrofters printed the memorial edition for Wise. Saint Benedict and Mary Baker Eddy close the teachers' span. Froebel founded the kindergarten, and Arnold led Rugby School in England.

Great scientists fill Hubbard's twelfth volume of little journeys. Sir Isaac Newton leads the contents list. Galileo and Copernicus follow as astronomy's revolutionaries. Humboldt and William Herschel widen the field further.

Charles Darwin and Haeckel bring evolution into the volume. Linnæus, Huxley, and John Tyndall represent classification and experiment. Alfred Russel Wallace and John Fiske close the roster. Hubbard visits each thinker's home to humanize abstract science. John Fiske closes a roster running from Newton to Wallace. Hubbard's scientists receive the same home-visit treatment as poets. Wallace reached the evolution idea on his own, far from Darwin.
moral-principles-and-medical-practice-th:
The Reverend Charles Coppens, a Jesuit, taught medical jurisprudence at Creighton Medical College in Omaha. Benziger Brothers published these lectures as the basis of medical jurisprudence. Coppens had already written textbooks on metaphysics, ethics, oratory, and rhetoric. He dedicates the volume to John A. Creighton, founder of the college and its hospital.

The lectures apply moral principles to medical practice. Doctors face questions of conscience that law alone cannot settle, and Coppens addresses them directly. A transcriber's note warns that the original numbering skips a paragraph in Lecture One. The book shows how Catholic moral theology entered American medical training at the bedside level.
nasa-tm-19630010658-an-investigation-of-:
Harry T. Norton, Jr., Willard E. Foss, Jr., and John M. Swihart of Langley wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-540. It tests clusters of small jet exits at supersonic speeds. A cluster replaces one large nozzle with several small ones. Changed layouts of the cluster are the study's focus.

Grouped exits can shorten an engine and ease cooling. They can also waste thrust if the jets interfere with each other. The team tried modified layouts and measured the results at speed. Rocket builders for large boosters weighed such clusters closely then. This work gave them test data, not just theory, on how jet groupings behave in fast flow.
nasa-tm-19650024119-low-intensity-decame:
J K Alexander and R G Stone at Goddard analyzed faint radio emissions from Jupiter at decameter wavelengths. Their data came from the Clark Lake Radio Observatory and its Christiansen-type array. They focused on very weak activity that stronger-burst studies tended to miss. The question was how the shape of a noise storm changes when faint events are counted.

Their study of activity against Jupiter's rotation longitude found the same general shape others reported. The peaks were somewhat broadened once weak events were included. That detail matters for locating the sources on Jupiter. Weak-signal work tests whether a pattern built from loud events still holds at the quiet end.
new-york-times-current-history-the-europ:
June 1915 forms number three of volume two in the New York Times Current History of the European War. The volume spans April to September 1915. This number leads with the Lusitania case, printed with a map. That sinking had pulled America close to the war.

President Wilson's speeches and his note to Germany anchor the number. A history traces a series of attacks on American lives in the German war zone. The American note to Germany is printed in full. So is the German Embassy's warning, with the German official report on what followed. Readers could judge both governments from their own words.
scientific-american-volume-22-no-1-janua: Volume XXII, Number 1, new series, of the weekly Scientific American is dated New York, January 1, 1870, at three dollars per annum in advance. A contents note marks illustrated articles with an asterisk. Listed items open with engines of the Spanish gunboats, the torpedo problem, and sugar making in Louisiana. Sticking or court plaster, an improved hoisting pulley, Ferdinand de Lesseps as chief promoter of the Suez Canal, and an ingenious vent peg follow, several of them illustrated.
scientific-american-volume-40-no-13-marc: Dated New York, March 29, 1879, this issue is Volume XL, Number 13, new series, of Scientific American, a weekly journal of practical information, art, science, mechanics, chemistry, and manufactures. Its masthead proclaims the paper established in 1845, edited and owned by Munn and Company at Number 37 Park Row, with O. D. Munn and A. E. Beach named. A year's subscription costs three dollars and twenty cents, postage prepaid. Club terms promise one free extra copy for every five subscribers. Readers are told to remit by postal order.
the-faithful-shepherdess-the-works-of-fr:
The Faithful Shepherdess is a pastoral play printed here in volume two of the works of Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher. Clorin, a shepherdess, opens the play alone at the grave of her dead love.

She vows to leave dances, games, and the company of maids and shepherds, and to live by the grave. Her one gift left is skill with herbs. She can cure wounds, snake stings, love-sickness, and madness, and gives her cures freely to men and beasts alike. Vowed chastity, grief, and healing art set the tone for the woodland tale of love and trial that follows.
